title: The nine obstacles (1.30–1.31)
hook: Patanjali lists, nearly two thousand years ago, exactly what goes wrong when people try to practice

segments.voice: Yesterday: om is his name. Repeat it, japa, again, and dwell on its meaning, and the obstacles disappear. Did om find its way into a red light or a queue? Today: which obstacles? Day four hundred thirty-eight.

Day one of a new habit: you're on fire. Day four: you have a cold. Day six: you're tired and skip it. Day nine: you wonder if any of this works. Day twelve: you had a great session, so you assume you've arrived, and stop paying attention. Day fifteen: the good feeling is gone and you can't get it back. Anyone who has tried to keep a practice knows this slide. Patanjali knew it too. In sutra 1.30 he names every step of it.
screen: `DAY ONE: ON FIRE.` → `A COLD. A SKIP. A DOUBT.` → `PATANJALI NAMES EVERY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here are the nine, from sutra 1.30. Vyadhi: illness. The body gets sick and practice stops. Styana: dullness, a mind that won't get going. Samshaya: doubt, is this even real? Pramada: carelessness, not tending the conditions. Alasya: laziness, heaviness of body and mind. Avirati: craving, the pull of the senses that won't let go. Bhranti darshana: false seeing, mistaking one thing for another, including mistaking a good moment for arrival. Alabdha bhumikatva: not reaching a stage, the plateau where nothing seems to move. And anavasthitatva: reaching a stage and failing to hold it. Patanjali calls these the scatterings of the mind. Then sutra 1.31 adds the companions that tend to show up with them, four signs you can feel in the body: pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and ragged breathing in and out. Two things stand out. First, how ordinary the list is. Illness and laziness sit right next to doubt and false seeing. The obstacles aren't demons. They're Tuesday. Second, the last two are about success, not failure: never getting to a new stage, and getting there and slipping off. Patanjali knows that a good day can be as much of a trap as a bad one. Naming them doesn't make them vanish. But it changes the story from I'm bad at this to oh, that's number three, doubt. And tomorrow's sutra gives the remedy.
screen: `ILLNESS, DULLNESS, DOUBT.` · `CARELESSNESS, LAZINESS, CRAVING.` · `FALSE SEEING, PLATEAUS, SLIPPING.` · then, large: `THE OBSTACLES ARE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle on the breath. As you sit, watch for any of the nine as they show up. Dullness: a heavy fog. Doubt: a voice asking what's the point. Craving: a sudden thought of food or your phone. Each time you spot one, name it kindly, like spotting a bird: there's doubt. There's dullness. Then come back to the breath. Notice the body too: is the breath ragged, is there restlessness? Name it and return. The bell holds the time.
The nine obstacles. Illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, false seeing, failing to reach a stage, and failing to hold one: Patanjali's list of what scatters the mind.

Your line: disease, doubt, laziness and the rest. Today, when you stall on something that matters to you, name which obstacle it is, out of the nine, before you decide what to do. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Yoga teachers often have students learn the nine antarayas by name, so that illness, doubt or a plateau can be recognized as a normal part of practice rather than a reason to quit.

pairs: reaching a stage and not holding it

myth: Patanjali's obstacles are all moral failings
illness is the first one. the list is ordinary: body, mind and habit.
two of the nine are about what happens around success
never reaching a stage, and reaching one but not holding it.
sutra 1.31 lists signs in the body that come with the obstacles
pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and ragged breathing.

fork.setup: you had a wonderful sit yesterday, and today you assume you've arrived and stop paying attention. which obstacle is this, most likely?
options: false seeing: mistaking a good moment for arrival.
fork.reveal: bhranti darshana, false seeing: taking one thing for another. a good moment taken for the goal is a classic case, and the slipping that follows is the ninth obstacle.

original.note: Sanskrit antarāya: obstacle, literally what comes in between. Patanjali names nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: obstacles are bad luck or weakness.
what it means: nine ordinary ways the mind gets scattered, from illness to losing a stage you'd reached.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa calls the nine chitta-vikshepas, scatterings of the mind, and 1.31 adds four 'companions' (sahabhuvah): pain, dejection, trembling and disturbed breath.

notes: Index carry is 'disease, doubt, laziness…' (with an ellipsis). The carry segment says it as 'disease, doubt, laziness and the rest'. The carry field matches the index exactly.
Renderings: avirati as craving/non-detachment; bhranti-darshana as false seeing; pramada as carelessness. Confirm.
'Nearly two thousand years ago' in the hook depends on dating (roughly 1,600–2,200 years); confirm or soften.
